comparison: Strong agreement on model fit findings. Both evaluations support that non-reversible models (NREV12) fit viral datasets better than reversible models. OpenEval emphasizes statistical rigor (LRT, AIC-c) while peer reviewers describe this as 'solid evidence' and note results are 'not surprising' given prior work. Nearly complete claim overlap (29/30 claims shared).

Both address simulation findings showing topology improvements with NREV12. OpenEval notes the paradoxical finding that topology improves while branch lengths worsen. Peer reviewers accept that NREV12 leads to trees 'closer to the true generating tree' with sufficient non-reversibility. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED, though they emphasize different aspects of the simulation results.

Partial overlap on simulation results. OpenEval focuses on DNR>8 threshold for significant improvement and limited practical benefit. Peer reviewers accept the broader simulation findings about NREV12 benefits. Both are SUPPORTED, but OpenEval provides more specific threshold analysis while peer review gives general acceptance.

Critical disagreement on practical recommendations. OpenEval finds recommendations 'appropriately cautious and well-supported' (SUPPORTED). Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, explicitly challenging the link between model fit and phylogenetic utility, stating 'I miss an experiment that links the two findings.' This represents the most significant divergence between evaluations.

Agreement on DNR characterization and strand-specific biases. OpenEval notes descriptive statistics are well-presented but lacks explanation for DNR-model preference disconnect. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these findings (no challenges raised) and note results are 'not surprising' biologically. Both SUPPORTED with high claim overlap (13 shared claims).

Both address strand-specific biases and biological mechanisms. OpenEval emphasizes NREV12 vs NREV6 comparison and dsRNA +strand exposure mechanism (SUPPORTED). Peer reviewers accept bias characterization implicitly. Moderate claim overlap (4 shared claims) with OpenEval providing more mechanistic detail.

Agreement on methodological soundness. OpenEval explicitly evaluates methods as clearly described with appropriate tools and adequate sample sizes (SUPPORTED). Peer reviewers implicitly accept methods through lack of critique, confirmed by editors' 'solid evidence' assessment. Both find empirical methods appropriate.

Agreement on simulation design quality. OpenEval finds simulation design appropriate with adequate replication and comprehensive DNR range (SUPPORTED). Peer reviewers implicitly accept simulation methodology as part of overall methods acceptance. Moderate claim overlap (5 shared claims) on simulation-specific methods.

OpenEval evaluates background/contextual claims from literature as SUPPORTED (well-established facts, appropriately cited). No corresponding peer review evaluation found - peer reviewers did not separately assess background literature claims.

OpenEval evaluates acknowledgment of knowledge gap about dsDNA/dsRNA mutation mechanisms as reasonable (SUPPORTED). No corresponding peer review evaluation found - this specific limitation was not separately addressed by peer reviewers.
